## LocalTrayTranslate v0.1.3

A correctness release. The typo-tolerant layer of the dictionary search could not return anything (the distance it computed for two identical words was 3, not 0), user entries containing a capital letter were invisible to the exact lookup, and a single clipboard hiccup or a corrupt database could take the whole tray application down. All three are fixed, plus the copy-on-selection path now waits for the modifiers of the hotkey to be released before it sends <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd>.

## Fixes

### The fuzzy layer never matched

The rolling-rows implementation of the optimal string alignment distance swapped its three buffers incorrectly: after the two assignments `prev` and `cur` referenced the *same* array, so every row overwrote the previous one and the function accumulated garbage. Measured against the old code:

| input | returned | correct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `word` / `word` | 3 | 0 |
| `wrod` / `word` | 4 | 1 |
| `helo` / `hello` | 3 | 1 |

Since the layer only keeps candidates within a small budget (1 edit for ≤4 characters, 2 up to 8, 3 beyond), and the query was compared without being lowercased, the last recall layer was effectively dead and the ranking above it was noise. The three-row rotation is now correct, the query is normalised once, and distances are computed once per candidate instead of twice.

### User entries with capitals were unfindable

`AddUserEntryAsync` / `UpdateUserEntryAsync` stored `normalized_word` through `NormalizeInput` — which only collapses whitespace — while every lookup compared against `NormalizeWord` (trim + lowercase). A user entry for `Apple`, `API` or `Hello` therefore never matched its own exact query. Both writes now use the same normalisation as the queries; entries already stored with a mixed-case key are still found through the translation/definition match, and are normalised the next time they are edited.

### Nothing caught an exception

There was no `DispatcherUnhandledException` handler, and every entry point — tray menu items, global hotkeys, the dictionary window — was an `async void` or `async` lambda. A clipboard held open by another program (`Clipboard.Clear` throws `COMException`), a failed `SendKeys`, a locked SQLite file or a failed OCR call terminated the process, tray icon included.

The app now has three layers: each hotkey/tray entry point has its own `try`/`catch`, `DispatcherUnhandledException` keeps the app alive, and `AppDomain.UnhandledException` logs what got past the first two. Dictionary initialisation at startup is guarded as well — a damaged or locked `dictionary.db` now reports and keeps running instead of preventing the app from starting.

### Copy-on-selection raced the hotkey's own modifiers

Pressing the hotkey (default <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>X</kbd>) left those keys physically down, so the synthetic <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> was delivered as <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> and many applications ignored it. The selection service now polls `GetAsyncKeyState` until Ctrl/Alt/Shift/Win are released (bounded by a timeout), then copies. Clipboard reads and writes retry on the transient "another application has the clipboard open" error, and the previous clipboard content is restored from a snapshot rather than from a lazily-bound OLE reference taken before the clear.

### Single instance

Two copies of the app meant two tray icons and a silently failed `RegisterHotKey`. A named mutex now makes the second instance exit immediately.

### Hotkey settings

- A combination without any modifier is refused: registering a bare letter as a global hotkey would swallow that key everywhere in Windows.
- The two actions can no longer be given the same combination (`RegisterHotKey` only succeeds once, so the second would silently not work).
- A registration failure is reported instead of looking like a successful save.

### Smaller corrections

- **Example sentences.** The ECDICT import put the `exchange` column (`p:went/d:gone`, or the raw `collins` / `bnc` number) into `example`, so the popup displayed "0" where a sentence was expected. ECDICT has no example field; the column stays empty rather than showing a fragment of morphology data.
- **CSV import.** The import dialog listed `*.csv`, but lines were split on tabs only, so a comma-separated file produced "no valid entries". The delimiter is detected from the first usable line; quoted CSV fields are handled.
- **Dictionary replacement.** A bundled dictionary replaces the local copy by size, and the old `-wal` / `-shm` sidecars are now deleted together with it — replaying a stale WAL against a new main file could corrupt the copy.
- **Build inputs stay out of the tree**: `dictionary.db` and `data/raw/` (the downloaded ECDICT / CC-CEDICT sources) are produced by `tools/` and are not committed; only `data/schema.sql` is.

## Downloads

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `LocalTrayTranslate-0.1.3-win-x64.zip` | Self-contained x64 build (`.NET 8` runtime included), unzip and run `LocalTrayTranslate.exe` |

## Notes

- Windows 10/11 x64. OCR uses the Windows OCR engine, so recognition languages follow the ones installed in *Settings → Language*.
- The zip carries the bundled `dictionary.db` (~180 MB) next to the executable. On first start it is copied into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\TranslateLite`; user entries live in `user_dictionary.db` in the same folder and are never touched by a dictionary update.
- Settings live in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\TranslateLite\settings.json` and are safe to edit by hand, or to delete to return to the defaults (<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>X</kbd> selection, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd> screen OCR).
